questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Pixelforja Games, a game studio with 40 developers, maintains a monorepo with the engine in C++, the editor tools in C#, the gameplay scripts in Lua, and a matchmaking backend in .NET. The team has adopted Claude Code to generate and refactor code across all of these subsystems. Constraints: each subsystem has its own conventions, the binary assets folder must never be modified by the AI, full builds take 40 minutes, and the studio wants the Claude Code configuration to be version-controlled and shared by the team. Automated tests are scattered across `Tests/` folders inside each subsystem (engine, tools, backend), and new `Tests/` folders appear every quarter. The team wants the testing conventions (naming, use of fixtures, a ban on `Thread.Sleep`) to be applied whenever Claude touches tests, without spending context when it works on other parts of the code. What is the BEST way to configure this?
opcoes: Create a `CLAUDE.md` inside each existing `Tests/` folder with the conventions, since subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load on demand.
Create a file in `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` frontmatter using a glob such as `**/Tests/**`, containing the testing conventions.
Add a "Testing conventions" section to the project's root `CLAUDE.md`, which is version-controlled and read by the whole team.
Create a `test-conventions` skill with a `description` saying to use it when editing tests, letting auto-loading decide.
questoes.explicacao: A convention that spans scattered directories and should apply only when those files are touched is the exact use case for `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` (glob). It covers future directories, doesn't duplicate content, and doesn't take up context needlessly.
feedbacks: Tempting because subdirectory CLAUDE.md files really do load on demand. But it duplicates the content across N folders, causes the copies to drift apart, and doesn't cover `Tests/` folders that appear in the future.
Correct. A rule with `paths:` loads only when files matching the glob are touched, automatically covers future `Tests/` folders, and avoids duplication.
It works to apply the rules, but it loads in every session, including when Claude is working on shaders or Lua, wasting context, which the question asked to avoid.
Tempting (skills load on demand), but loading a skill based on its `description` is the model's decision, i.e., probabilistic. A rule with `paths:` is triggered deterministically by the file path.

questoes.pergunta: At Pixelforja, the developer Caio wants Claude, in this monorepo only, to use the path of his machine's test sandbox (`D:/sandbox-caio`) and to respond more briefly. In his other projects these preferences make no sense, and the rest of the team should not receive them. Where should he put these instructions?
opcoes: In `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, the user's personal instructions file, which does not go into the repository.
In the project's `CLAUDE.md`, in a "Caio only" section.
In `.claude/settings.local.json`, the personal settings file that git ignores.
In `CLAUDE.local.md` at the project root, which is personal and stays out of version control.
questoes.explicacao: The CLAUDE.md hierarchy has an exact level for "personal + this project only": `CLAUDE.local.md` (gitignored). `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is personal but global, the project's CLAUDE.md belongs to the team, and settings files hold configuration, not instructions.
feedbacks: Tempting because it's personal, but it applies to all of Caio's projects, and he said these preferences make no sense outside this monorepo.
It goes into git and is read by the whole team. It depends on the model obeying an "only for" in plain text, and it pollutes everyone's context.
Naming trap: the file is personal and gitignored, but it holds configuration (permissions, hooks, env), not natural-language instructions for the model.
Correct. `CLAUDE.local.md` is the personal, project-specific level: it doesn't go into git and doesn't leak into Caio's other projects.

questoes.pergunta: Pixelforja needs to migrate the engine's Lua binding layer from one library to another. The change touches about 60 files in C++ and Lua, and there are at least two valid strategies (a temporary adapter or a direct migration). What is the FIRST thing the developer should do in Claude Code?
opcoes: Enter plan mode and approve a plan before any edits.
Turn on `acceptEdits` and ask for the direct migration, relying on the test suite to catch regressions in each subsystem.
Spawn one subagent per file, in parallel, to migrate the 60 files at the same time.
First write a `/migrate-binding` skill with the migration steps for the team to reuse.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode exists for large, multi-file changes involving an architectural decision and more than one valid approach. The first thing is to explore and plan with approval; execution (even in parallel) comes afterward.
feedbacks: Correct. A multi-file change with an architectural decision and several valid approaches is the classic case for plan mode: explore and design before editing.
Tempting for its speed, but it skips the decision between the strategies and turns 60 files into trial and error with 40-minute builds. Tests don't replace choosing an approach.
Parallelizing before a plan exists spreads inconsistent decisions across 60 files (each subagent chooses on its own). Parallelism can come later, executing an approved plan.
It inverts the order: it's not yet known which strategy to use. A skill is for a known, repeatable procedure, not for a one-off migration that is still undefined.

questoes.pergunta: Pixelforja has the `/audit-shaders` skill, which reads hundreds of shader files and produces a 20-line report. After each use, the main conversation is clogged with shader content and Claude starts responding worse for the rest of the session. What is the SIMPLEST fix that solves this?
opcoes: Add `disable-model-invocation: true` to the skill's frontmatter.
Create a custom subagent in `.claude/agents/` for the audit and rewrite the skill to delegate to it.
Add `context: fork` to the frontmatter, so the skill runs in an isolated subagent and returns only the report.
Instruct the team to run `/compact` right after each use of the skill, to summarize the shader content left in the conversation.
questoes.explicacao: `context: fork` makes the skill run in an isolated subagent, without the conversation history, and return only the result. It's the simplest way to move noisy work out of the main conversation.
feedbacks: Tempting because it touches the frontmatter, but it only prevents auto-loading by the model. When the developer calls `/audit-shaders`, the reading still happens in the main conversation.
It would work, but it's more work than necessary: the skill itself can already run in isolation with `context: fork`. The exam rewards the simplest fix that solves the problem.
Correct. With `context: fork`, the heavy reading happens in an isolated context and only the result comes back to the conversation. It's one line of frontmatter.

A reactive, manual remedy: the context has already been polluted, the summary loses details, and it depends on each developer remembering. It doesn't address the cause (the reading happening in the main context).

questoes.pergunta: At Pixelforja there are `.claude/commands/build.md` (old) and `.claude/skills/build/SKILL.md` (new), both version-controlled. A developer edits `commands/build.md` to change the build target, but `/build` keeps behaving the old way. What is the most likely explanation?
opcoes: Files in `.claude/commands/` have been deprecated and are no longer read by Claude Code.
Commands are cached and are only re-read after the developer reinstalls Claude Code.
Both define `/build`, and in that conflict the skill takes precedence over the command.
A personal command `~/.claude/commands/build.md` always overrides project commands.
questoes.explicacao: `.claude/commands/x.md` and `.claude/skills/x/SKILL.md` create the same `/x`. In a conflict, the skill wins. It's a common gotcha since commands were merged into skills.
feedbacks: Tempting because commands were merged into skills, but `.claude/commands/` still works. The problem here is the name conflict, not deprecation.
An explanation invented to fit the symptom. Even after reloading, `/build` would resolve to the skill, which takes precedence.
Correct. Commands were merged into skills; with the same name, the skill wins. Edit the SKILL.md or remove the duplicate.
It mixes up the priority order (personal above project) with the case presented: nothing points to a personal command, and the conflict described is within the project itself.

questoes.pergunta: Pixelforja wants a `/release-notes` skill that (1) runs only when a developer explicitly calls it, never on Claude's own initiative, and (2) has access only to reading git and writing the notes file. Which frontmatter fields meet these two requirements? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: `disable-model-invocation: true`
`user-invocable: false`
`context: fork`
`allowed-tools` listing only the necessary tools (git read commands and writing the file).
`when_to_use: "use only when the user explicitly asks"`
questoes.explicacao: The invocation requirement is met by a deterministic field (`disable-model-invocation`), not by description text. The access requirement is met by `allowed-tools`. `user-invocable: false` is the opposite of what was asked.
feedbacks: Correct. It prevents the model from loading the skill on its own; it remains available to the user via `/release-notes`.
Trap: it does the opposite of what was asked. It hides the skill from the user (it leaves the `/` menu) and lets only the model invoke it.
Useful for isolating context, but it doesn't control who invokes the skill or which tools it uses.
Correct. It restricts the tools the skill can use while it is active, meeting requirement (2).
Tempting, but it's text that guides auto-loading, i.e., probabilistic. To guarantee the model never invokes it, use `disable-model-invocation`.

questoes.pergunta: Part of the Pixelforja team uses another coding agent and maintains a detailed `AGENTS.md`. The repository also has a `CLAUDE.md` with Claude Code-specific instructions. The developers notice that Claude doesn't follow anything in `AGENTS.md`. What is the SIMPLEST fix that doesn't lose either file's content?
opcoes: Add `@AGENTS.md` to `CLAUDE.md`, importing the shared content.
Delete `CLAUDE.md`, since Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` when there is no CLAUDE.md.
Copy the content of `AGENTS.md` into `CLAUDE.md`.
Move the content of `AGENTS.md` into a file in `.claude/rules/` without frontmatter.
questoes.explicacao: With both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md present, Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md. To share instructions across agents without duplication, import with `@AGENTS.md`.
feedbacks: Correct. With both files present, CLAUDE.md wins and AGENTS.md is not read on its own. The `@import` brings in the content without duplicating it.
It makes AGENTS.md get read, but it loses the Claude Code-specific instructions, which the question forbids.
It works today, but it creates two copies that will diverge at the next edit. The import solves it without duplication.
It would load at the start of the session, but it removes the content from the file the other agent reads, and breaks the workflow of the other part of the team.

questoes.pergunta: At Pixelforja, the `CLAUDE.md` says in capital letters: "NEVER modify files in `Assets/Binary/` and NEVER run `git push --force`". Even so, during a long session Claude ran a `git push --force` on a shared branch. What should the team do?
opcoes: Rewrite the rule in CLAUDE.md with examples and repeat it in a `.claude/rules/` file without frontmatter.
Configure a `PostToolUse` hook that detects the `push --force` or the edit in `Assets/Binary/` and automatically restores the previous state.
Require everyone to always work in plan mode, approving each step manually.
A `PreToolUse` hook in the project settings that blocks these commands and edits before execution (exit 2 / `deny`).
questoes.explicacao: A prompt instruction has a non-zero failure rate. For a destructive or critical action, the guarantee comes from a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks before execution. `PostToolUse` is too late for irreversible actions.
feedbacks: It reinforces the prompt, but it is still probabilistic. There has already been one failure, and for a destructive action "less likely" isn't enough.
Tempting because it's a hook, but `PostToolUse` runs after the action has happened. A force push on a shared branch may have already affected other people.
It creates enormous friction and depends on human attention at every approval. That isn't enforcement, it's manual review.
Correct. A critical rule goes into deterministic code. A `PreToolUse` hook prevents the action before it happens, regardless of what the model decides.

questoes.pergunta: A Pixelforja developer spent the morning in a session in which Claude analyzed the rendering pipeline in depth (the files haven't changed since). Now he wants to test two different refactoring strategies starting from that same analysis, without one attempt contaminating the other. What should he do?
opcoes: Run `--resume <id>` in two terminals, one for each strategy.
Use `--resume <id> --fork-session` for each strategy, creating two branches from the same base.
Open two new sessions, one per strategy, and paste a detailed summary of the morning's analysis into each one.
Continue in the same session, test the first strategy, run `/compact`, and then test the second.
questoes.explicacao: Tool results still valid → resume. To explore alternatives from a common base without contamination → `--fork-session`, which generates a new ID per branch.
feedbacks: Tempting, but both would continue the same session. Without `--fork-session`, the attempts are not isolated.
Correct. `--fork-session` creates a new ID from the shared history. Each branch inherits the still-valid analysis and doesn't contaminate the other.
It works, but it throws away an analysis that is still valid (the files haven't changed), and the summary loses details. A new session with a summary is for when the context has become stale.
Both attempts end up in the same history, and the summary of the first contaminates the second, which is what the developer wanted to avoid.

questoes.pergunta: Yesterday, a Pixelforja developer left a Claude Code session in the middle of work on the matchmaking backend. Overnight, a colleague merged a refactoring that rewrote 30 of the files Claude had read and analyzed. What is the BEST way to continue?
opcoes: Use `--resume` and continue normally, since Claude re-reads files when it needs to edit them.
Use `--resume <id> --fork-session` so as not to contaminate the original session.
Use `--resume` and ask Claude to re-read all 30 files before continuing.
Start a new session, passing in a structured summary of the decisions and conclusions that remain valid.
questoes.explicacao: `--resume` is appropriate when tool results are still valid. If a lot has changed, start fresh with a structured summary. (With small changes, you can resume and state explicitly what changed.)
feedbacks: The history is still full of old reads of the 30 files, and the model may reason about the old code without noticing.
`--fork-session` isolates branches, but the fork inherits the same stale reads. It doesn't solve the stale-context problem.
It updates the code, but it leaves the old and new versions side by side in the context, bloating the window and opening the door to confusion. With this much change, a new session is cleaner.
Correct. With a large share of the tool results stale, the old history hurts more than it helps. A new session with a structured summary starts from a clean base.

questoes.pergunta: Pixelforja uses Claude to generate Lua functions for NPC behavior. The tech lead wrote three paragraphs describing the desired style (state names, transition structure, how to log), but the generated code keeps interpreting the description differently each time. Which change tends to deliver the GREATEST gain in consistency?
opcoes: Expand the prose description, detailing each convention, the special cases, and the exceptions the team has already identified.
Include 2–3 concrete examples of input (the NPC specification) and output (a Lua function in the expected style).
Raise `effort` to the maximum, so the model thinks more about each function.
Add a second Claude call that reviews each function and fixes the style.
questoes.explicacao: For format and style, 2–3 concrete, varied input/output examples beat prose instructions. It's the first iterative refinement technique to try before adding extra models.
feedbacks: More prose tends to create more ways to interpret it. The problem is the ambiguity of the description, not a lack of text.
Correct. Concrete input/output examples show the pattern unambiguously and work better than prose for locking in format and style.
More effort doesn't fix an ambiguous specification: the model thinks harder about a description that still allows several readings.
It adds cost and latency to fix a symptom. The reviewer would have the same problem: the style specification is still ambiguous.

questoes.pergunta: At Pixelforja, Claude reviews the generated Lua code and flags issues in the "non-idiomatic code" category. This category has so many false positives that the developers have started ignoring the alerts from the good categories too (memory leaks, nil access). The prompt says only "point out non-idiomatic code, use your good judgment". What is the BEST course of action?
opcoes: Ask the model for a confidence score and show only findings with confidence above 0.8.
Replace "use your good judgment" with "be conservative and only flag when you are certain".
Turn off the noisy category, rewrite the criterion with what counts, what doesn't count, and borderline cases, and turn it back on after measuring.
Keep the category and add a second model that filters out false positives before the alerts reach the developers, preserving coverage.
questoes.explicacao: Vague criteria ("good judgment", "conservative") produce inconsistency. Define what counts, what doesn't count, and borderline examples, and turn off the noisy category while you refine it, so it doesn't contaminate trust in the others.
feedbacks: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated. The problem is the vague criterion, and a threshold on an uncalibrated number only hides the symptom.
It swaps one vague instruction for another. "Conservative" still doesn't say what counts and what doesn't, so the result remains inconsistent.
Correct. The noisy category erodes trust in the good ones. First stop the damage, then refine with explicit criteria, and only then turn it back on.
More complex than necessary, and it keeps the vague criterion at the source. The simplest fix is to make the criterion explicit.

questoes.pergunta: At Pixelforja, Claude tries to replace `return null;` with `return Result.Empty;` in a single method of a generated 3,000-line C# file, but the `Edit` tool fails, saying the snippet is not unique: the same line appears 14 times in the file. What should Claude do?
opcoes: Expand `old_string` with neighboring lines from that method until the snippet is unique, and retry the `Edit`.
Retry the `Edit` with `replace_all: true`.
Use `Bash` with `sed` to make the replacement directly in the file, without depending on `Edit`'s uniqueness requirement.
Use `Write` to rewrite the entire file with the change already applied, based on the file content Claude remembers.
questoes.explicacao: `Edit` fails when the snippet is not unique. The fix is to expand the snippet until it is unique (or read the file and rewrite it carefully). `replace_all` and `sed` change too many occurrences.
feedbacks: Correct. `Edit` requires a unique snippet. Expanding the context pinpoints exactly the right occurrence without affecting the others.
Tempting because it makes the error go away, but it changes all 14 occurrences, and only one should change. It trades a visible error for a silent bug.
It bypasses `Edit`'s uniqueness safeguard. A `sed` without a precise address also changes all 14 occurrences or requires a fragile regex.
In a 3,000-line file, rewriting from memory risks losing or altering sections. If you are going to rewrite, you must read the whole file first; here, expanding the snippet is simpler and safer.

questoes.pergunta: After three hours in a Pixelforja session optimizing the ECS system, Claude started answering with "typical ECS patterns" instead of citing the project's classes, and forgot decisions made at the beginning (e.g., no allocation in the hot path). What is the BEST action?
opcoes: Record decisions and findings in a scratchpad file and run a proactive `/compact` with a structured summary.
Switch to a model with a 1M-token window, so the entire session fits without needing to compact anything.
Repeat the important decisions at the start of every new message, so they always stay recent in the context.
Run `/clear` and start over without any prior context.
questoes.explicacao: Signs of degradation (generic answers, forgotten decisions) call for state persisted in a scratchpad file and a proactive `/compact` with a structured summary, or a new session started from that file.
feedbacks: Correct. A scratchpad file survives compression, and compacting proactively with a structured summary tackles long-context degradation.
A larger window doesn't eliminate "lost in the middle", costs more on every turn, and only postpones the problem.
It helps occasionally, but it's manual, prone to being forgotten, and bloats every turn. It doesn't organize the state persistently.
It clears the degradation, but it throws away all the findings and decisions. The state should have been persisted before clearing.

questoes.pergunta: During long optimization work at Pixelforja, after a `/compact` Claude lost exact numbers that were acceptance criteria (a budget of 16.6 ms per frame, 4 MB of allocation per scene) and the IDs of the related bug tickets. Which measures prevent this from happening again? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Ask in the chat: "always remember 16.6 ms and 4 MB".
Record these values and IDs in a persistent file (e.g., task notes referenced in CLAUDE.md).
Disable auto-compaction and never compact the session.
Increase the responses' `max_tokens` so the summary generated during compaction has room for more numeric detail.
Pass instructions to `/compact` explicitly asking it to preserve the budget numbers and the ticket IDs.
questoes.explicacao: Summaries lose exact values, IDs, and numbers. Protect them outside the history (a file, CLAUDE.md, a facts block) and, when compacting, state explicitly what to preserve.
feedbacks: The message itself goes into the history and can be summarized at the next compaction, which is exactly what happened.
Correct. Whatever must not be lost goes into a file/memory. Files and CLAUDE.md survive compaction; the scrollback doesn't.
It trades loss of detail for long-context degradation and an eventual window overflow. It's not a solution.
`max_tokens` limits the output of each response; it doesn't decide what survives compaction. It targets the wrong mechanism.
Correct. `/compact` accepts focus instructions, and asking it to preserve exact values reduces the loss that summarization usually causes.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Verdana Insights, an ESG consultancy, produces due diligence reports on the sustainability claims of listed companies. The system is multi-agent: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to subagents for web search, document analysis (sustainability reports in PDF), emissions database queries, and synthesis. Constraints: every claim in the report must be traceable to its source (clients audit them), reports go out within 48h, and the cost per report is monitored. For the question "assess the ESG practices of the mining company Rocha Alta", the final report covered emissions and water use in detail, but said nothing about governance or community impacts. The logs show that all subagents completed their tasks without errors, and the synthesis used everything it received. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The web search subagent has poor tool descriptions and therefore didn't find sources on governance and communities.
The synthesis subagent discarded the social and governance parts for lack of space in the context window.
Overly narrow decomposition by the coordinator (environmental subtasks only), with no explicit coverage check.
The analysis subagents ran sequentially, and the deadline ran out before they got to governance.
questoes.explicacao: When all subagents perform well and coverage is still missing, the problem lies in the coordinator's decomposition. The fix is to decompose more broadly and check coverage explicitly.
feedbacks: Tempting, but the logs show that no subagent received a task about governance. You can't blame the search for something that was never requested.
The question says the synthesis used everything it received. The S and G content never reached it.
Correct. Successful subagents and a complete synthesis point to the decomposition: the S and G subtasks were never created.
Nothing in the logs indicates a timeout: they all completed. Inventing an operational cause strays from the evidence.

questoes.pergunta: In Verdana's system, the coordinator spawns 4 independent search subagents (one per source), but the trace shows they run one after another, and the step takes four times longer than it should. What is the fix?
opcoes: Increase the concurrent subagent limit in the runtime settings.
Emit the 4 `Agent` tool calls in the same coordinator response.
Move the searches to the Batch API, which processes requests in parallel.
Merge the 4 subagents into a single subagent with all the search tools.
questoes.explicacao: Parallel subagents = multiple `Agent` `tool_use` blocks in the same coordinator response. Separate turns = sequential execution.
feedbacks: Tempting, but the bottleneck isn't the limit: the coordinator only requests one subagent at a time, so there's nothing to run in parallel.
Correct. Subagent parallelism comes from multiple `Agent` calls in the same response. One per turn is, by definition, sequential.
Batch has a window of up to 24h, with no SLA, and doesn't support a multi-turn tool loop. It worsens the latency of an interactive step.
It eliminates parallelism instead of enabling it, and inflates the number of tools in a single agent.

questoes.pergunta: At Verdana, the coordinator delegates to the document analysis subagent with the prompt "analyze the report as we discussed and say whether the targets are credible". The subagent returns a generic text ("the company appears to have ambitious targets"). The coordinator's context already holds 120k tokens of results from other subagents. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Replace the subagent with a fork, which inherits the coordinator's entire conversation and thus understands what was "discussed" without needing to repeat anything.
Give the analysis subagent access to the web search tools so it can figure out the context on its own.
Increase the subagent's `max_tokens` so it produces a longer, more detailed analysis.
Explicitly pass the company, the document, the period, the targets to verify, and the criteria in the prompt, asking for structured output.
questoes.explicacao: A subagent's context does not inherit the coordinator's history. "As we discussed" fails. For a bounded task, pass everything explicitly. A fork is for when the task truly needs the whole conversation.
feedbacks: Tempting, because the fork solves the lack of context. But it carries 120k tokens of results from other subagents, which don't matter for this analysis and dilute attention. For a bounded, well-specifiable task, a fresh subagent with an explicit prompt is better.
It makes the subagent guess what the coordinator already knows, wasting calls and risking analyzing the wrong thing.
A longer answer without context is still generic. The problem is the input, not the size of the output.
Correct. A fresh subagent has an isolated context: everything it needs must go explicitly into the prompt. For a bounded task, a complete prompt is the way to go.

questoes.pergunta: A Verdana analyst spent two hours in Claude Code building up, together with the model, a detailed understanding of a client's constraints (sector exclusions, preferred methodology, legal caveats). Now she wants a side exploration (comparing three reporting frameworks) that depends on all of those nuances. She wants to receive only the conclusion back in the main conversation, without polluting it, and at the lowest possible cost. What is most appropriate?
opcoes: Create a fresh subagent and write in the prompt a summary of the client constraints built up in the session.
Use a fork, which inherits the conversation, reuses the prompt cache, and returns only the result.
Open another terminal with `--resume <id> --fork-session` and do the comparison in that separate branch of the session.
Do the comparison in the main conversation itself and run `/compact` at the end.
questoes.explicacao: A fork inherits the whole conversation and shares the cache: it's the right choice when the subtask needs the accumulated context. A fresh subagent is for a bounded task that can be specified in the prompt. `--fork-session` creates a separate session branch, whose result doesn't come back on its own.
feedbacks: It's the right choice for a well-bounded task, but here the value lies in the nuances that a summary loses. Moreover, the fresh subagent has a separate cache, so it costs more.
Correct. The task depends on the accumulated nuances, so inheriting the conversation is the point. The fork shares the cache (cheaper) and only the conclusion comes back.
Tempting (it also inherits the history and doesn't contaminate), but the conclusion stays in another session and doesn't come back to the main conversation, as the analyst wanted.
It pollutes the main conversation with the side work, and `/compact` also summarizes, lossily, what was built up before.

questoes.pergunta: To save latency at Verdana, an engineer proposes that the emissions database subagent send the numbers directly to the synthesis subagent, without going through the coordinator. What is the BEST assessment?
opcoes: Keep everything going through the coordinator, which handles errors, controls what reaches the synthesis, and redelegates the gaps it finds.
Accept it, as long as both subagents write to a shared memory file that the coordinator can audit later.
Accept it and create a message bus so that any subagent can talk to any other.
Merge the emissions and synthesis subagents into a single agent, eliminating the data handoff.
questoes.explicacao: In hub-and-spoke, subagents don't talk to each other directly. The coordinator routes, aggregates, handles errors, and redelegates. Direct communication is an anti-pattern even when it seems faster.
feedbacks: Correct. Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator routes all communication, which provides observability, consistent error handling, and quality control.
Tempting (it seems to preserve traceability), but the audit only comes after the fact: the coordinator loses the chance to handle errors and gaps before the synthesis.
It generalizes the anti-pattern: direct communication between subagents, more complexity, and no central point for error handling.
It mixes responsibilities and increases that agent's tools, and the latency gain from one pass through the coordinator rarely justifies it.

questoes.pergunta: Verdana has two workflows: (1) the monthly emissions bulletin for 50 companies, always with the same steps (collect → normalize units → compare with the previous month → format); and (2) the investigation of a greenwashing allegation, in which the next step depends on what is found (a document may lead to a subsidiary, which leads to a lawsuit...). Which combination of strategies is most appropriate?
opcoes: Dynamic decomposition for both, for flexibility.
Prompt chaining for both, because fixed steps are more auditable.
Dynamic decomposition for the bulletin and prompt chaining for the investigation.
Prompt chaining for the bulletin and dynamic decomposition for the investigation.
questoes.explicacao: Chaining = fixed, sequential steps known in advance. Dynamic decomposition = subtasks emerge from the findings (open-ended investigation).
feedbacks: Flexibility in a fixed workflow only adds variability and cost. The bulletin becomes less predictable with no gain at all.
Auditability is desirable, but in the investigation the steps are not known in advance. A fixed chain can't follow the leads.
It inverts the two: it puts adaptability where the steps are fixed and rigidity where they emerge from the findings.
Correct. Fixed steps known in advance call for chaining. An open-ended investigation, in which subtasks emerge from the findings, calls for dynamic decomposition.

questoes.pergunta: At Verdana, the coordinator receives a report's synthesis and notices there is no 2022 emissions data and no independent source for the net zero target. Which coordinator behaviors are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Rerun the entire pipeline, with twice as many subagents and sources, to increase the chance of covering all the gaps at once.
Ask the synthesis subagent to estimate 2022 by interpolating 2021 and 2023, marking the value as "estimated" in the report.
Evaluate the synthesis against explicit coverage criteria and list the concrete gaps.
Launch a second round targeted only at the gaps and re-synthesize.
Publish the report as is, since the synthesis didn't report any errors.
questoes.explicacao: Iterative refinement: run the subagents → evaluate → identify gaps → targeted second round → synthesize. No rerunning the entire pipeline and no filling gaps with estimates.
feedbacks: Cost and time multiplied to redo what was already fine. Invoke only the subagents the gap requires.
Tempting (the gap gets "filled" and labeled), but it fabricates data in a report the client audits. A gap with no source should be searched for or declared.
Correct. Iterative refinement starts by evaluating and identifying the gaps explicitly.
Correct. The second round is targeted: only the subagents the gaps require.
The absence of errors is not complete coverage. The coordinator exists precisely to detect gaps and redelegate.

questoes.pergunta: In a Verdana report on the company Litoral Têxtil, the final text said "no environmental controversies found". It was later discovered that the news search tool had timed out and returned `{"results": []}` as a success. What is the MOST appropriate fix in the tool?
opcoes: Have the coordinator automatically retry, up to three times, any search that comes back empty before accepting the result as true.
Add to the synthesis prompt: "if there are no results, write that no data is available".
Return a structured error on timeout (transient category, retryable, query attempted), reserving empty for "nothing found".
Increase the search tool's timeout to 60 seconds.
questoes.explicacao: Silent suppression (an error turned into an empty list returned as success) is an anti-pattern. Errors should be structured, and retryable when transient. A 200 with an empty array only when the search actually ran.
feedbacks: It treats the symptom in the wrong place: it wastes calls retrying searches that legitimately found nothing and still doesn't distinguish a failure from a result.
It improves the wording, but it still doesn't know the search failed. "No data" and "nothing found" are still conflated.
Correct. Empty is information ("nothing found"); a timeout is a search that didn't run. The tool needs to distinguish the two in a structured way.
It reduces the frequency, but the next timeout will still become a silent "nothing found". The error suppression remains.

questoes.pergunta: At Verdana, the synthesis subagent was given the same 16 tools as the rest of the system (search, fetch, database queries, citation formatting, etc.). It frequently fires off new searches in the middle of the synthesis and sometimes uses the wrong tool to format citations. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Rewrite the descriptions of the 16 tools to make it clear when each one should be used and how it differs from similar ones.
Use `tool_choice: none` throughout the synthesis step, to prevent it from firing off new searches in the middle of the text.
Give the synthesis only the few tools of its role, leaving search and queries to the specialized subagents.
Enable tool search with `defer_loading` on the synthesis's 16 tools.
questoes.explicacao: Too many tools, and tools outside the agent's role, degrade selection. Restrict each subagent to the tools of its function (4–5); improving descriptions alone isn't enough.
feedbacks: It helps, but it isn't enough: the problem is the agent having tools that don't match its role. Improving descriptions alone doesn't fix having too many tools.
Tempting (nobody searches if no tool can be called), but it also blocks the tools the synthesis needs, such as citation formatting.
Correct. With 4–5 tools per agent at decision time, selection improves. If the synthesis finds gaps, it reports them to the coordinator instead of searching on its own.
Tool search is for large catalogs. Here the problem is one of role, not size: deferred or not, the synthesis still has access to search tools.

questoes.pergunta: At Verdana, the emissions database subagent receives two errors in the same run: `429 Too Many Requests` from a public database and `403 token expired` from the paid database. Which handling is correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: For the 429, the subagent itself retries with backoff and only propagates it to the coordinator if it keeps failing.
For the 403, retry with exponential backoff up to 5 times before giving up, since tokens can be renewed.
For the 403, propagate a structured, non-retryable permission error to the coordinator for escalation.
Propagate both errors to the coordinator immediately, without trying anything locally.
Treat both as "no data" and proceed with the report, so as not to delay delivery.
questoes.explicacao: Transient (429, timeout) → local retry with backoff. Permission (403, expired token) → non-retryable; propagate it in structured form for escalation. Never silence it.
feedbacks: Correct. A rate limit is transient and retryable. Local recovery avoids bothering the coordinator with something that resolves itself.
A permission error is not transient: all 5 attempts will fail the same way, wasting time and possibly triggering lockouts.
Correct. An expired token is a permission error: retrying doesn't help, so it should go up with context for someone to resolve.
It dumps on the coordinator a transient error that the subagent would resolve with backoff. Local recovery is the subagent's responsibility.
Silent suppression: the report would go out saying there is no data when, in fact, the query failed.

questoes.pergunta: For the same metric (Rocha Alta's 2023 scope 1 emissions), the company's sustainability report says 1.2 Mt CO2e and the regulator's database says 1.5 Mt CO2e. How should Verdana's synthesis handle this?
opcoes: Use the regulator's value, since it's the official and independent source, and cite only that source in the report.
Report the average of the two, 1.35 Mt CO2e, citing both sources in a footnote.
Use the most recently published value, assuming it corrects the earlier one.
Show both values with source and date, labeling the data point as contested.
questoes.explicacao: Conflict between sources: annotate the diverging values with their sources and label it as contested. Don't silently pick one or take an average.
feedbacks: Tempting (the official source is usually more reliable), but it silently discards the conflict. The divergence between what the company declares and the regulator is precisely the due diligence finding.
An average creates a number that no source asserts. Citing both sources doesn't make the value traceable.
It assumes a correction without evidence. Publication date doesn't resolve a conflict for the same period.
Correct. A conflict between sources is annotated with the diverging values and their sources, without silently picking one. The client audits and needs to see the divergence.

questoes.pergunta: Verdana's synthesis started flagging a "contradiction" between one subagent that reported 2.1 Mt of emissions and another that reported 1.8 Mt for the same company. On investigating, the team saw that these were 2021 and 2023 figures, but the subagents return only running text ("the company emits 2.1 Mt"). What is the fix at the source?
opcoes: Have the subagents return structured findings with value, reference period, publication date, and source.
Instruct the synthesis to ignore differences smaller than 20% between sources, treating them as normal methodological variation.
Deduplicate the findings in the synthesis, always keeping the most recent one.
Send every detected "contradiction" to human review before publication.
questoes.explicacao: Temporal data needs "data as of", publication, and collection dates. Numbers from different periods are not a contradiction. Structured handoff separates content from metadata to preserve provenance.
feedbacks: Correct. With the period explicit, the synthesis sees that they are different years (not a contradiction), and the attribution survives all the way to the report.
It hides small real conflicts and doesn't solve the cause: the synthesis still doesn't know which period each number is from.
It throws away the historical series, which is useful information, and still lacks the metadata to distinguish a real conflict from a different period.
Human review is expensive and here it handles a false alarm created by missing metadata. Fix the source first.

questoes.pergunta: Verdana's coordinator aggregates the outputs of 12 subagents (about 8k tokens each, in running text) before the synthesis. The final reports have been omitting findings that were in the outputs of the subagents in the middle of the list. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Switch to a model with a 1M-token window.
Subagents return condensed, structured findings; the synthesis receives headers by topic and the key findings at the beginning.
Add to the synthesis prompt: "read all sections carefully, including those in the middle, before concluding".
Run the synthesis twice, with the subagent outputs in reverse order, and merge the two results into a single final report.
questoes.explicacao: Lost in the middle: cut the volume (only the relevant fields), put the key findings at the beginning, and use section headers. A larger window doesn't solve it.
feedbacks: The input already fits in the window. The problem is attention to the middle sections, which gets worse with more volume, not better.
Correct. This tackles "lost in the middle": less volume, key findings at the beginning, and structure with headers.
A generic instruction doesn't change how attention is distributed across a long, disorganized context.
It doubles the cost and creates a new merging and conflict problem. It doesn't address the volume or the lack of structure.

questoes.pergunta: At Verdana, the synthesis labels claims with certainty levels, but inconsistently: a claim supported only by the company's own report sometimes comes out as "high certainty". The prompt says "classify the certainty of each claim according to your judgment". What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Ask the model for a numeric score from 0 to 1 for each claim and map ranges of that score to the labels.
Set `temperature` to zero to make the classification deterministic.
Add a second model that reclassifies the certainty of each claim before the report goes on to the end client.
Define explicit criteria per label (e.g., established = 2+ independent sources), with borderline examples.
questoes.explicacao: Explicit criteria (what counts, what doesn't count, borderline examples) beat "use your judgment" and self-reported scores. It's the simplest fix before adding models.
feedbacks: It swaps a vague judgment for a self-reported, poorly calibrated number. The criterion remains undefined.
Being deterministic is not being correct: the same vague criterion would always produce the same error. And on newer models `temperature` may not even be accepted.
More complex and with the same root problem: nobody defined what each level means. Explicit criteria come before "one model checking another".
Correct. Replacing "your judgment" with explicit criteria for what counts, what doesn't count, and the borderline cases makes the labeling consistent.

questoes.pergunta: Verdana's subagents returned findings by calling the `report_findings` tool with `tool_choice: {"type":"tool","name":"report_findings"}`. When migrating to a newer model, these requests started returning HTTP 400. The only goal of forcing the tool was to guarantee output in the schema's format. Which alternatives solve this? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Switch to `tool_choice: any`, which requires the model to call some tool without naming which one, and keep only `report_findings` declared.
Use structured outputs (`output_config.format` with `json_schema`) for the subagent's final response.
Prefill the assistant response with `{` to force JSON output.
Use `tool_choice: auto`, with an explicit instruction naming the `report_findings` tool and `strict: true` in its definition.
Remove the tool and ask in the system prompt: "respond only in valid JSON".
questoes.explicacao: On newer models, `any` and a forced `tool` return 400 [volatile, check the model's capabilities]. Substitutes: structured outputs, or `auto` + an instruction naming the tool + `strict: true`. Prefill also returns 400.
feedbacks: Trap: on newer models, `any` also returns 400, just like the forced `tool`.
Correct. When forcing existed only to get JSON in the schema's format, structured outputs is the direct substitute on newer models.
Assistant prefill also returns 400 on newer models. The recommendation is to use structured outputs.
Correct. It's the recommended alternative for models that reject forcing: the instruction steers the call and `strict` guarantees the input's conformance.
It goes back to free text: malformed JSON, missing fields, and wrong types. It loses the schema guarantee that was the goal.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Corrente Energia, an electric power distribution company, has a platform team that uses Claude Code and an internal assistant (built with the Agent SDK) to speed up developers on a legacy billing system with about 2 million lines of C# and integrations. MCP servers provide access to Jira, Grafana, and a read-only replica of the customer database. Constraints: customers' personal data (CPF, address) must not appear in sessions, secrets must not go into git, and the team wants to reduce onboarding time for new developers. A newly arrived developer asks Claude Code "how is the tariff calculated under the red tariff flag?". Claude starts reading entire directories of the billing module, and the context fills up before any answer. Which exploration strategy should Claude follow?
opcoes: Use Glob to list all the `*.cs` files in the billing module and read them in alphabetical order.
Switch to a model with a 1M-token window and load the entire module at once.
Grep for the likely entry points (e.g., "CalculateTariff"), read what it finds, and follow imports with new Greps.
First ask Claude to generate an architecture document for the entire system and only then answer the developer's question.
questoes.explicacao: Codebase exploration: grep for the entry points → read → follow imports with grep → read. Reading everything up front (or loading everything into a giant window) is the anti-pattern.
feedbacks: It's an organized version of the anti-pattern of reading everything up front. Glob finds files by name, not by relevant content.
Expensive, suffers from "lost in the middle", and 2 million lines still wouldn't fit. Volume is no substitute for targeted search.
Correct. Grep → Read → follow imports with Grep → Read: incremental understanding, spending context only on what matters.
It spends hours and context on a broad artifact to answer a specific question. It inverts the order of targeted exploration.

questoes.pergunta: At Corrente Energia, two MCP servers expose similar tools: `search_logs` (Grafana Loki, "searches logs") and `query_logs` (audit platform, "queries logs"). Claude frequently looks for invoice audit trails in Loki and for application errors in the audit platform. What is the SIMPLEST fix?
opcoes: Create a classifier that reads the developer's request and decides which MCP server to route to before Claude chooses the tool.
Rename and re-describe the tools to separate their purposes, stating when to use each one and how they differ.
Disconnect the audit server, leaving only Loki, to eliminate the ambiguity between the tools once and for all.
Instruct in CLAUDE.md: "when in doubt, call both tools and compare".
questoes.explicacao: Overlapping tools with nearly identical descriptions cause misrouting. First fix: rename and describe them to separate their purposes (or merge the tools). A classifier comes later, if still needed.
feedbacks: It adds a component to solve what a better description solves. The exam rewards the simplest fix.
Correct. The description is the selection criterion. Separating purposes, with "when to use" and "how it differs", fixes the misrouting between overlapping tools.
It ends the ambiguity by losing a necessary capability: the audit trails become inaccessible.
It doubles the calls and context consumption, and still leaves the model deciding with descriptions that don't explain the difference.

questoes.pergunta: The Corrente Energia team is organizing the installation scopes of the MCP servers in Claude Code. Which statements are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The local MCP scope is written to `.claude/settings.local.json`, the project's personal, gitignored file.
The user scope writes the servers to a `.mcp.json` in the user's home directory, applying to all projects.
A server added with local scope is registered in `~/.claude.json`, applies only to this project, and is not shared with the team.
A server declared in the project's `.mcp.json` can override the configuration of a server enforced by the managed scope.
Servers declared in the project's `.mcp.json` ask for user approval before being used in an interactive session.
questoes.explicacao: MCP scopes: local (default, personal, this project, `~/.claude.json`) · project (`.mcp.json`, version-controlled, requires approval) · user (all your projects, `~/.claude.json`) · managed (organization).
feedbacks: Classic trap: the name "local" is misleading. The local MCP scope lives in `~/.claude.json`, not in `settings.local.json`.
The user scope also lives in `~/.claude.json`. `.mcp.json` is the project-scope file, at the repository root.
Correct. The local scope (the default) is personal and project-specific, and it lives in `~/.claude.json`.
Managed is the organization's configuration, pushed by the admin. The project doesn't override what the managed policy enforces.
Correct. Because they arrive via git, project servers require approval. It's a safeguard against servers slipped into the repository.

questoes.pergunta: Corrente Energia's internal assistant (Agent SDK) was connected to 7 MCP servers, totaling about 120 tools and 60k tokens of definitions. The cost per request went up and tool selection got worse. Most questions always use the same 4 tools. What is the BEST approach?
opcoes: Enable tool search, with `defer_loading` on the catalog, keeping the 3–5 most-used tools loaded (not deferred).
Mark all 120 tools with `defer_loading`, so nothing takes up context until it's needed.
Shorten the descriptions of the 120 tools to reduce the tokens in the definitions.
Create 7 subagents, one per MCP server, and a coordinator that decides which one to delegate each question to.
questoes.explicacao: Tool search (`defer_loading`) is recommended with 10+ tools, large definitions, or several MCP servers. Keep the 3–5 most frequent ones non-deferred. It reconciles a large catalog with few tools visible at decision time.
feedbacks: Correct. A large catalog and several MCP servers is the use case for tool search: the model sees few tools at decision time, loads the rest on demand, and the prompt cache is preserved.
Tempting, but at least one tool must remain non-deferred, and deferring the 4 most-used ones adds a search step to almost every question.
It reduces cost and makes selection even worse: the description is the criterion for choosing the tool.
It may make sense in other contexts, but it's a heavy restructuring for a problem that tool search solves directly, and it splits by server, not by function.

questoes.pergunta:
At Corrente Energia, the version-controlled `.mcp.json` has this entry for Jira, and the server fails to connect for the whole team:
`"jira": { "url": "https://mcp.jira.corrente.example/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${JIRA_TOKEN}" } }`
Everyone has `JIRA_TOKEN` set in their environment. What is the FIRST fix to make?
opcoes: Add `"type": "http"` to the entry.
Replace `${JIRA_TOKEN}` with the literal token value, since variable expansion doesn't work in headers.
Add `"type": "sse"`, which is the transport for remote servers.
Move the entry to the user scope with `claude mcp add` on each machine.
questoes.explicacao: `.mcp.json` gotcha: a `url` without `type` is read as stdio. Declare `"type": "http"` (Streamable HTTP) for remote servers and keep secrets in `${VAR}`.
feedbacks: Correct. An entry with a `url` but no `type` is interpreted as stdio and fails. A remote server must declare its `type`.
`${VAR}` expansion works in `.mcp.json` and is precisely the right way. A literal token in a version-controlled file leaks the secret.
SSE is legacy. For a current remote server, use Streamable HTTP (`"http"`), which is also the remote transport that supports OAuth.
It doesn't fix the problem (the `type` would still be missing) and it also undoes the git-based sharing the team wants.

questoes.pergunta: A Corrente Energia developer wants to know every place where the `WHITE_TARIFF_V2` feature flag is read across the 2 million lines, to assess the impact of removing it. A quick Grep shows more than 400 scattered occurrences. He wants to keep working in the same session afterward. What is most appropriate?
opcoes: Run the Grep in the main session and ask Claude to read each of the 400 occurrences.
Delegate the investigation to an Explore subagent, which does the searches and reads in its own context and returns only a summary of the impact.
Enter plan mode so that the investigation doesn't modify files.
Do the investigation in the main session and run `/compact` as soon as it's done.
questoes.explicacao: Bounded, noisy work (a high-volume search) → a subagent (Explore) that returns only the conclusion. It's the classic context mitigation in a large codebase.
feedbacks: It works, but it fills the main conversation with hundreds of snippets, degrading the rest of the session.
Correct. A high-volume, noisy search goes to a subagent. The main conversation receives only the conclusion and stays clean.
Plan mode prevents edits, but the reading still happens in the main context. The problem is context, not editing.
A remedy after the damage: the summary loses details of the analysis itself and of everything that came before.

questoes.pergunta: Corrente Energia wants a reusable "security reviewer": Claude should be able to delegate to it when there are sensitive changes, it can only read code (no editing or running commands), it uses a specific model, and the definition must be shared with the whole team via git. What is the BEST way?
opcoes: Create `~/.claude/agents/security-reviewer.md` with the same configuration.
Add a section to CLAUDE.md: "When reviewing security, act as a reviewer and don't edit files or run commands".
Create `.claude/agents/security-reviewer.md` with `description`, `tools: Read, Grep, Glob`, and `model`, version-controlled.
Create a `/review-security` skill without tools frontmatter, describing the reviewer's role and checklist in detail.
questoes.explicacao: A reusable, delegable agent with restricted tools and its own model = a custom subagent in `.claude/agents/` (project, version-controlled). `~/.claude/agents/` is personal.
feedbacks: The configuration is right, but the location is personal: the subagent doesn't reach the team via git.
It doesn't isolate context, restrict tools, or change the model. "Don't edit" in a prompt is probabilistic.
Correct. A custom subagent in `.claude/agents/` (project, version-controlled) meets all the requirements: delegation by description, restricted tools, its own model, isolated context.

A skill with no tool restrictions and no model of its own doesn't guarantee the reviewer only reads. The requirement is a delegable agent with restricted tools, which is the role of `.claude/agents/`.

questoes.pergunta: At Corrente Energia, half the team uses Claude Code through the VS Code extension, some use the JetBrains one, and the rest use the CLI. The tech lead asks how to ensure that the project's CLAUDE.md, skills, settings, and MCP servers apply to everyone. What is the correct answer?
opcoes: Replicate the configuration in each IDE's settings files (`.vscode/settings.json` and `.idea/`).
Standardize the team on the CLI, because IDE extensions don't load project skills or MCP servers.
Use CLAUDE.md for instructions and configure skills and MCP separately on each surface, which keeps its own registry.
Keep the configuration in the repository: all surfaces use the same engine and read the same files.
questoes.explicacao: All Claude Code surfaces use the same engine: the project's CLAUDE.md, settings, skills, and MCP apply on all of them.
feedbacks: It creates copies that will diverge. The extensions read the same Claude Code configuration as the CLI.
False premise: the extensions use the same engine and load skills and MCP normally.
A half-truth that creates work and divergence: skills and MCP are also project configuration, common to all surfaces.
Correct. The CLI, IDE extensions, desktop, and web share the same engine, so the project configuration applies equally on all of them.

questoes.pergunta: A Corrente Energia developer complains that he has to manually approve every run of `dotnet test` and `git status` in Claude Code, dozens of times a day. The team wants to solve this for everyone without giving up approval prompts for risky commands. What is the BEST configuration?
opcoes: Run sessions with `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, since the repository is internal and version-controlled.
Specific `allow` rules for these commands in the project's `.claude/settings.json`.
Use `acceptEdits` mode.
Create a `PreToolUse` hook that returns `allow` for any Bash call made inside the repository.
questoes.explicacao: Granular permissions (`allow` for specific commands) in the project settings remove the friction without opening everything up. `bypassPermissions` and a hook that approves everything are too broad, and `acceptEdits` covers only edits.
feedbacks: It solves the annoyance by removing all protections, including for destructive commands. It's not for routine use.
Correct. Granular permission rules allow only what is safe and repetitive, shared via the project settings. Everything else still asks for approval.
Tempting because of its name, but `acceptEdits` automatically approves file edits, not Bash commands like `dotnet test`.
It allows all of Bash, including risky commands, which the team wants to avoid.

questoes.pergunta: Corrente Energia's platform team is documenting, for onboarding, how Claude Code's instruction hierarchy works. Which statements are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: An `@import` inside CLAUDE.md resolves the path relative to the file that contains the import.
The user's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` takes precedence over the organization's managed policy instructions.
All CLAUDE.md files in the repository's subdirectories are loaded at the start of the session when it is opened at the root.
A `CLAUDE.local.md` is version-controlled with the project, so the team shares each developer's personal preferences.
The `CLAUDE.md` in a subdirectory such as `billing/` is loaded on demand, when Claude reads files from that directory.
questoes.explicacao: Hierarchy: managed policy → user → project → CLAUDE.local.md → subdirectory (on demand). `@import` is relative to the importing file, and `CLAUDE.local.md` is personal and stays out of git.
feedbacks: Correct. `@import` paths are relative to the importing file (`@~/` points to the home directory).
It inverts the hierarchy: the managed policy is the organization level and is not overridden by the user.
Only the files at the root and in the levels above load at the start. Subdirectory files come in on demand.
Naming trap: `CLAUDE.local.md` is personal and stays out of git. Team instructions go in the project's CLAUDE.md.
Correct. A subdirectory CLAUDE.md doesn't load at the start of the session; it comes in when files in that folder are accessed.

questoes.pergunta: The MCP server for Corrente Energia's customer database replica returns rows with CPF and address. The team needs to guarantee that this data never enters Claude's context, but the developers need the other columns to debug invoices. Which mechanism is most appropriate?
opcoes: A `PreToolUse` hook that blocks any query to the customers table made through the replica's MCP server.
A rule in CLAUDE.md and in the system prompt: "never display customers' CPF or address in responses".
A `UserPromptSubmit` hook that removes CPFs typed by developers in their prompts.
A `PostToolUse` hook on that MCP server's tools that masks CPF and address before the model sees the result.
questoes.explicacao: `PostToolUse` normalizes, cleans, and annotates tool results (e.g., masking PII) before the model reasons about them. `PreToolUse` decides whether the call happens; a prompt guarantees nothing.
feedbacks: Deterministic, but it blocks too much: the developers lose the columns they need. The problem is in the result, not in the call.
Probabilistic and too late: the data has already entered the context, and the rule only tries to prevent it from being repeated.
It targets the wrong input: the PII comes from the tool result, not from what the developer types.
Correct. `PostToolUse` is the point for normalizing and cleaning tool results, such as masking PII, deterministically and without losing the useful columns.

questoes.pergunta: Corrente Energia's security team requires a hook that prevents any Claude Code session, by any developer and in any company repository, from reading `.env` and `*.pfx` files. No developer may disable it. Where should this hook be configured?
opcoes: In the `.claude/settings.json` of each company repository.
In the `~/.claude/settings.json` on each machine, installed by an onboarding script.
In the managed settings (managed policy) distributed by the organization.
In the frontmatter of a security skill that every repository must include.
questoes.explicacao: Hooks can live in user, project, or local settings, or in the managed policy. An organizational rule that nobody can disable → managed policy.
feedbacks: It's shared via git, but it has to be replicated repository by repository, can be removed in a commit, and doesn't cover new or personal repositories.
It applies to all projects on that machine, but the developer can edit or delete the file. It doesn't satisfy "nobody can disable it".
Correct. The managed policy is the organization level: it applies to everyone and cannot be overridden by user or project settings.
Skill hooks only apply while the skill is active. It's not a permanent barrier for all sessions.

questoes.pergunta: Corrente Energia wants an onboarding bot in Slack that answers questions about the code: it needs to read files, run grep, delegate searches to subagents, and respect security hooks. By policy, the source code cannot leave the company's infrastructure. Which way of building it is most appropriate?
opcoes: Claude Agent SDK, running on the company's infrastructure (it comes with file tools, subagents, and hooks ready to use).
A manual agentic loop on top of the Messages API, implementing the read, grep, and subagent tools from scratch.
The client SDK's Tool Runner, registering read and grep functions.
Managed Agents, which already hosts the agentic loop and an execution sandbox ready to run the tools.
questoes.explicacao: From simplest to most ready-made: manual loop, Tool Runner, Managed Agents (hosted), Agent SDK (the Claude Code harness as a library, which you host). Choose the simplest one that meets all the requirements.
feedbacks: Correct. The SDK comes with exactly what the bot needs (built-in tools, subagents, hooks) ready to use, and it runs wherever the company wants to host it.
Possible, but it reimplements what the Agent SDK already provides. It's not the simplest option that meets the requirements.
It runs the loop for your tools, but it doesn't come with subagents or hooks. Explicit requirements would be missing.
Tempting because it's the most ready-made option, but the sandbox is hosted outside the company, and the policy forbids the code from leaving the infrastructure.

questoes.pergunta: The `query_metrics` tool on the Grafana MCP server returns, for each series, a JSON with about 40 metadata fields and 2,000 data points. After just a few questions, the Corrente Energia assistant's context fills up and large MCP output warnings appear. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Raise the MCP output token limit (`MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`) so the results aren't truncated.
Switch the assistant's model to one with a larger window.
Make the tool return only the relevant fields and aggregated data, with detail on demand.
Instruct the model, in the system prompt, to ignore the metadata fields and look only at the series' data points.
questoes.explicacao: Trim the tool output: return the relevant fields, not all 40. Raising limits or windows only lets more noise in.
feedbacks: Tempting because the warning goes away, but it lets even more tokens into the context. It treats the symptom in the wrong direction.
It postpones the problem, makes every turn more expensive, and worsens "lost in the middle" with thousands of irrelevant data points.
Correct. Trimming tool output at the source (only what matters for the decision) is the direct fix for context consumption.
The tokens have already been consumed by the time the model "ignores" them. An instruction doesn't reduce the size of the result.

questoes.pergunta: The Corrente Energia assistant (Agent SDK) runs long incident investigation tasks, with hundreds of tool calls. Old results (logs and queries already analyzed) dominate the context, but the investigation's reasoning and decisions must remain intact, without paraphrasing. Which server-side mechanism is most appropriate?
opcoes: Context editing, clearing old tool results and keeping the rest of the conversation.
Compaction, summarizing all the prior context into one block.
Memory tool, writing the tool results to persistent files outside the conversation.
Increase `max_tokens` to give the model more room to respond at each step of the investigation.
questoes.explicacao: Context editing clears old tool results (good for verbose loops). Compaction summarizes everything (good when the narrative can be condensed). The memory tool persists across sessions.
feedbacks: Correct. Context editing removes what weighs the most (old tool results) without summarizing the narrative, which is what must stay intact.
Tempting (it reduces context), but it also summarizes the reasoning and decisions, which the question requires to stay intact. Compaction is for when the narrative can be condensed.
The memory tool is for persisting findings across sessions. It doesn't remove from the context the results that are already there.
`max_tokens` is the output ceiling; it doesn't free up space in the input context. Wrong mechanism.

questoes.pergunta: Scenario: Banco Atalaia, an investment bank, extracts data from term sheets, prospectuses, and trade confirmations (including scanned PDFs with handwritten annotations) to feed its risk system in JSON. The volume is about 200,000 documents per month, most of them processed overnight. Constraints: every extracted value must match the source document, missing fields must not be invented, the compliance department audits samples, and the risk system rejects JSON that doesn't conform to the schema. Many term sheets have no maturity date (they are perpetual), but the extracted JSON always comes back with a plausible, invented `maturity_date`. The schema defines `maturity_date` as a required string. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Enable `strict: true` to guarantee that the output follows the schema.
Make the field nullable and return `null` when the date is not present.
Add a retry loop that asks the model to check the date against the document.
Add few-shot examples of term sheets with the maturity date correctly filled in from the document.
questoes.explicacao: For data that may be missing, use a nullable field in the schema and instruct the model to return `null`. A required, non-null field pushes the model to invent, and `strict` only guarantees the format.
feedbacks: Tempting, but it makes things worse: with the field required and non-nullable, `strict` guarantees that the date always comes back, i.e., that it gets invented. Schema conformance is not correctness.
Correct. A required field with no null option pushes the model to invent. A nullable field provides a legitimate way out for the missing data.
A retry doesn't recover information that isn't in the source. As long as the schema demands a date, the model still has no honest way out.
Examples with the field always filled in reinforce the always-fill pattern. What's missing are examples of the absent case and, before that, a schema that allows it.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia wants to guarantee that `coupon_rate` stays between 0 and 100 and that `isin` follows the 12-character pattern (2 letters + 9 alphanumerics + 1 digit). The team put `minimum`/`maximum` on `coupon_rate` and a simple `pattern` on `isin` in the raw schema used with structured outputs, and the API started rejecting the request with HTTP 400. What is the correct approach?
opcoes: Replace the constraints with a `oneOf` listing the valid ISIN formats.
Turn off strict, because then the model will respect `minimum`, `maximum`, and `pattern`.
Describe the rules only in each property's `description`, which the model reads when generating each JSON field.
Keep the ISIN `pattern`, remove `minimum`/`maximum` from the schema, and validate the range in code, with specific errors in a retry.
questoes.explicacao: Strict doesn't support numeric ranges (`minimum`/`maximum`), string length, array constraints, or recursion: in a raw schema, these give a 400. A `pattern` with a simple regex is supported. The range goes into code, with a retry that reports the specific error.
feedbacks: `oneOf` is not among the constructs documented as supported, and it doesn't address the `coupon_rate` range, which is the cause of the 400.
It treats the symptom: without strict the 400 goes away, but the schema becomes guidance, the range is still not guaranteed, and structural conformance is lost.
A description helps the model, but it's probabilistic. A rule that the risk system requires calls for deterministic validation in code.
Correct. The simple ISIN `pattern` is supported; numeric ranges are not. Whatever the schema doesn't support is enforced in code.

questoes.pergunta: At Banco Atalaia, the extracted trade confirmations pass the schema, but in 2% of them the `total_amount` field doesn't match the sum of `items[].amount`. Sometimes the document really does contain a diverging total (a broker error), which compliance wants to flag. What is the BEST design?
opcoes: Have the model calculate `total_amount` as the sum of the items, guaranteeing that the two fields always match in the JSON.
Enable `strict: true` on the extraction, so the API rejects any JSON with inconsistent totals.
Ask in the prompt for the model to double-check the sum before responding.
Extract the stated total, calculate the sum of the items in code, and flag the discrepancy.
questoes.explicacao: Valid schema ≠ correct data. Extract the stated value and calculate the expected value in code to detect discrepancies, distinguishing an extraction error from an error in the source.
feedbacks: It hides exactly what compliance wants to see: a wrong total in the document would be silently "corrected".
Schema conformance is not semantic correctness. Strict guarantees types and fields, not that a sum is right.
Probabilistic, and it conflates the two cases: the model may "correct" a total that was wrong in the document.
Correct. Extracting the stated value and the calculated one separates a model error from a document error. Semantic validation lives in code.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia implemented a validation loop with retry for the extraction. When validation fails, the code resends the document with the message "the previous extraction had errors, try again", and the retry success rate is low. Which change has the GREATEST impact?
opcoes: Increase the maximum number of attempts from 2 to 6, giving the model more chances to get the extraction right.
Include the specific errors in the retry (field, value read, expected value), with an attempt limit and explicit failure.
Raise `effort` on the retry, keeping the generic message.
On the retry, use another, more capable model to redo the document's extraction from scratch with the same prompt.
questoes.explicacao: Validation loop: extract → validate → return the specific errors → retry up to a limit → then fail with an error. A generic message wastes the retry.
feedbacks: More attempts with the same vague message repeat the same error at a higher cost.
Correct. A retry works when the model knows exactly what to fix. With a limit and explicit failure, the loop is neither infinite nor silent.
More effort without knowing what's wrong makes the model re-check everything blindly. The missing information is the concrete error.
It starts over from scratch without the diagnosis already obtained. The second model may make mistakes elsewhere, and nothing guarantees convergence.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia's legacy extraction code prefilled the assistant response with `{` to force JSON. When migrating to a newer model, every request started returning HTTP 400. The extraction doesn't perform any action; it only needs to return the JSON. What is the recommended fix?
opcoes: Remove the prefill and use structured outputs with the extraction's `json_schema`.
Move the `{` to the end of the system prompt, with the instruction "continue from here".
Replace the prefill with `tool_choice: any` with an extraction tool.
Keep the prefill and set `stop_sequences: ["}"]` to cut the response off at the end of the JSON.
questoes.explicacao: Assistant prefill returns 400 on newer models [volatile]. When migrating, test the shape of the request. For JSON in the schema's format, use structured outputs.
feedbacks: Correct. Assistant prefill returns 400 on newer models. To get JSON guaranteed to match the schema, structured outputs is the way to go.
An improvised workaround: it doesn't force anything and goes back to free text, with no schema guarantee.
On newer models, `any` also returns 400. It trades one 400 for another.
The 400 comes from the prefill, not from the end of the response. And cutting at the first `}` would break any JSON with nested objects.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia's `instrument_type` field is an enum `["CDB", "LCI", "debenture", "CRI"]`. With the arrival of COEs and structured notes, these documents started being forcibly classified as "debenture", and some illegible documents also get a guessed type. What is the BEST schema change?
opcoes: Expand the enum with all ~80 instrument types the market knows.
Replace the enum with a free-form string, letting the model write the type.
Add "other" (+ a detail field) and "unclear" to the enum.
Keep the enum and add few-shot examples of COEs classified as "debenture".
questoes.explicacao: Schema patterns: an enum with "other" + a detail field for unanticipated cases, and an "unclear"-type option to avoid guessing.
feedbacks: A giant enum that's always incomplete: the next new product runs into the same problem, and illegible documents still get guessed.
It loses the standardization the risk system needs ("Debenture", "debenture", "DEB"...).
Correct. "other" + detail accommodates new types without losing information, and "unclear" provides an honest way out when the document doesn't allow a decision.
It formally teaches the wrong classification. Few-shot is no substitute for a category missing from the schema.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia processes the day's documents in a nightly batch via the Batch API. In yesterday's batch of 40,000 requests, 3% ended as `errored` and 1% as `expired`. What is the correct next step?
opcoes: Resubmit in a new batch only the `custom_id`s with `errored` or `expired`, after investigating the `errored` ones.
Resubmit the entire batch of 40,000 requests to guarantee consistency.
Reprocess the 4% through the synchronous API immediately, without looking at the cause of the errors.
Match the results to the documents by the order of the input file and resubmit starting from the first one that failed.
questoes.explicacao: Batch API: `succeeded`/`errored`/`canceled`/`expired` states; results out of order (match by `custom_id`); resubmit only the ones that failed.
feedbacks: Correct. Resubmit only what failed and always match by `custom_id`, because the results don't come back in order.
It pays again for the 96% of the work that already succeeded and still risks new `expired` results.
It might even be acceptable given the small volume, but skipping the investigation of the `errored` ones repeats the same failures at full price.
Batch results come back out of order. Matching by position associates results with the wrong documents.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia is deciding which extraction workloads should go to the Batch API. Which are good candidates? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Extracting data from a term sheet while the trader waits at the desk to price the deal.
Reprocessing the archive of 2 million old prospectuses after a schema change.
The nightly extraction of the documents received during the day, consumed by the risk system the next morning.
An extraction in which, for each document, the model calls the `lookup_isin` tool and decides the next steps based on the result.
The compliance check that must approve the order before it is sent to the exchange.
questoes.explicacao: Batch: overnight analysis, mass reprocessing, periodic reports. Not: real time, a blocking step, a multi-turn tool loop within a request.
feedbacks: Real time: batch has no SLA and can take up to 24h.
Correct. Mass processing with no urgency is the classic batch use case (50% cheaper, window of up to 24h).
