Correct. A generous deadline and nothing waiting in real time: it fits within the batch window.
Tempting because of the volume, but a batch request doesn't support a multi-turn tool loop. The workflow would have to be redesigned.
A blocking step: it can't be at the mercy of a window of up to 24h with no SLA.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia uses the `record_extraction` tool, whose `input_schema` is the extraction structure itself. When `strict: true` was enabled on the tool, the API started rejecting the definition. The schema has optional fields (such as `maturity_date`) outside of `required` and doesn't declare `additionalProperties`. What fixes it?
opcoes: Remove the enums from the schema, because strict doesn't support `enum`.
Set `tool_choice` to force `record_extraction`, since strict only applies when the tool is forced.
Declare `additionalProperties: false`; preferably, move the optional fields into `required` as nullable.
Shorten the tool's `description`, because long descriptions are rejected under strict.
questoes.explicacao: `strict: true` requires `additionalProperties: false` on every object; that's what is missing. Optional properties are allowed, but they count toward a per-request limit [volatile]; the recommendation is `required` + nullable.
feedbacks: `enum` (of simple values) is supported under strict. The cause is the missing `additionalProperties: false`.
Strict doesn't depend on forcing the tool. Moreover, on newer models forcing returns 400.
Correct. Without `additionalProperties: false`, strict rejects the schema. Optional fields themselves are accepted, but `required` + nullable is the recommended practice.
Description length has nothing to do with strict validation. Rich descriptions are, in fact, recommended.

questoes.pergunta: During Banco Atalaia's extraction, the model calls the `lookup_isin` tool to validate the code it found. When the ISIN doesn't exist in the registry, the tool returns `{"error": "Operation failed"}`, and the model repeats the same call several times until it hits the iteration limit. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Lower the loop's iteration limit to 2, so the agent gives up on the validation sooner.
Instruct in the prompt: "if `lookup_isin` fails, don't try again; move on to the next field".
Make the tool return `{"results": []}` when the ISIN doesn't exist, instead of an error message.
Return a structured error: category "ISIN not found", `isRetryable: false`, and the ISIN that was looked up.
questoes.explicacao: A generic error ("Operation failed") hides the diagnosis and induces useless retries. A structured error with a category and `isRetryable` enables the right recovery.
feedbacks: An iteration limit is a backstop, not the primary mechanism. The model still doesn't know why it failed.
It also prevents retries on transient failures, where trying again is the right thing to do. The problem is that the error doesn't say what kind it is.
Better than "Operation failed", but an empty result with no context can be confused with a failed query. A structured error with a category is clearer.
Correct. With the category and the non-retryable flag, the model understands that repeating won't help and chooses another path.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia's extraction agent ends the loop when the response contains the text "EXTRACTION COMPLETE". On some documents, the model writes that phrase and, in the same response, emits a `tool_use` for `lookup_isin`. The loop ends, and the JSON goes out without the validation. What is the fix?
opcoes: Instruct the model to write "EXTRACTION COMPLETE" only after finishing all tool calls.
Decide whether to continue based on `stop_reason`: if it's `tool_use`, run the tools and return the `tool_result`s; end only on `end_turn`.
End the loop when the phrase appears and there is no `tool_use` block in the response.
Fix the loop at 10 iterations and use the last response as the result.
questoes.explicacao: Drive the loop by `stop_reason` (`tool_use` → run and continue; `end_turn` → finished). Having text doesn't mean it's finished.
feedbacks: It keeps the anti-pattern of driving the loop by reading natural language, just hoping the model obeys.
Correct. `content` can mix text and `tool_use`. `stop_reason` is the reliable signal of the loop's state.

Tempting (it fixes the reported case), but it still depends on a phrase. If the model finishes without writing it, or with different wording, the loop doesn't close. `stop_reason` already provides that information.
A fixed limit as the primary stopping mechanism is an anti-pattern. It cuts off long extractions and wastes iterations on short ones.

questoes.pergunta: Some Banco Atalaia extractions arrive with HTTP 200, but the JSON comes back incomplete or empty, and the code records the missing fields as `null`, as if the document didn't contain them. What check is missing?
opcoes: Treat as errors only responses with an HTTP status other than 200.
Check `stop_reason` before using the content, treating truncation and `refusal` as failures, not as extractions.
Wrap the JSON parse in try/catch and fill in the missing fields with `null`, logging a warning.
Increase the client's HTTP timeout so that long responses reach the extraction code complete.
questoes.explicacao: `refusal`, `max_tokens`, and `model_context_window_exceeded` arrive with HTTP 200. Check `stop_reason` before reading `content`, or truncation becomes a "success" with missing data.
feedbacks: That's exactly what already happens: these cases come with a 200 and get through.
Correct. Truncation and refusal arrive with HTTP 200. Without checking `stop_reason`, the code confuses "cut off" or "refused" with "missing data".
It formalizes silent suppression: it turns truncation into "field absent from the document", which violates the constraint against inventing absences.
The cutoff isn't a network one, it's a generation one (token limit or refusal). A longer timeout doesn't change the `stop_reason`.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia runs an agent that extracts clauses from 300-page prospectuses in several steps. To control cost, the team lowered `max_tokens`, and now several runs end with the JSON cut off in the middle. The team wants the model to organize itself to finish within a budget. What is the BEST approach?
opcoes: Lower `max_tokens` even further and stitch the cut-off parts together in code, asking for a continuation at each cutoff.
Add "be concise, you have little room to respond" to the prompt and keep `max_tokens` low.
Use a task budget (a ceiling visible to the model), leaving `max_tokens` only as a safety ceiling.
Limit the agent's number of turns to control the total cost.
questoes.explicacao: Task budget (visible, the model organizes itself) vs. `max_tokens` (invisible, cuts off in the middle). To control cost without truncating, use the visible budget and leave `max_tokens` as a backstop [task budget: volatile, beta].
feedbacks: More cutoffs and more fragile stitching. The model still doesn't know about the limit.
Vague and probabilistic: "little room" doesn't say how much, and the `max_tokens` cutoff remains invisible to the model.
Correct. A task budget is visible: the model organizes itself to fit. `max_tokens` is invisible and cuts off in the middle, so it serves as a backstop, not as cost control.
Limiting turns is a backstop and cuts the work off in the middle just the same. It doesn't let the model plan within a budget.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia measures 97% aggregate extraction accuracy and wants to reduce human review. A compliance audit, however, found recurring errors in documents with handwritten annotations. Which actions are the MOST appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Keep uniform sampling of 5% of all documents, since it's statistically unbiased.
Send to human review only the documents in which the model declares confidence below 0.7 on some extracted field.
Increase the number of retries in the validation loop for all documents.
Break down accuracy by document type and by field, to find segments performing much worse than the average.
Human review with risk-stratified sampling (more samples where the risk or the error rate is higher).
questoes.explicacao: An aggregate metric masks failures by document type or field; break it down by segment. Human review: risk-stratified sampling, not uniform sampling or self-reported confidence.
feedbacks: Tempting because of its "impartiality", but it spends review on stable segments and undersamples the handwritten documents, which is where the problem is.
Self-reported, uncalibrated confidence is a poor routing signal. The model may be confidently wrong precisely on the handwritten documents.
A retry doesn't recover information the model misread in an illegible handwritten note, and it makes the entire volume more expensive.
Correct. The aggregate metric hides failures by segment: 97% overall can coexist with 45% on handwritten notes.
Correct. Stratified sampling concentrates review where errors are most likely or most costly.

questoes.pergunta: Banco Atalaia wants to automatically approve extracted fields with high confidence and send the rest to human review. The model already returns a confidence score per field. What is the FIRST thing to do before using that score as a routing rule?
opcoes: Calibrate the scores against a labeled set, by document type and field, before defining thresholds.
Choose a conservative threshold, such as 0.95, to compensate for the lack of calibration and reduce wrong approvals.
Ask the model to justify each score in writing, to make the numbers more reliable and auditable.
Run the extraction twice and use the average of the two scores for each field.
questoes.explicacao: Per-field confidence is useful for routing, but only after it has been calibrated against a labeled set. Without calibration, the self-reported score means nothing.
feedbacks: Correct. Per-field confidence only means something after it has been calibrated against labeled data. Without that, the threshold is arbitrary.
A higher number on an uncalibrated scale is still arbitrary: it may approve confident errors and send correct answers to review.
The justification doesn't calibrate the number. The model rationalizes the score it has already given.
It doubles the cost and measures consistency, not accuracy. Two poorly calibrated scores remain poorly calibrated.
